radar.headline: 16 times the training length in state tracking, a playable game world at 60 FPS on one GPU, and inference 77% cheaper through the vocabulary

items.name: CEL
items.headline: 96 Robots Learn From Each Other
items.what: Collective experience learning: robots in the field share what they learn to improve one shared policy.
items.how: When a robot fails, a method called **FERT** finds the moment it went wrong and pulls similar stretches of trajectory from the fleet's shared successes; their actions become new training data, with no extra demonstrations or human corrections.
items.when: When a fleet outgrows its operators; across five real tasks, success ran from 93.3% to 99.2%.

number.says: phone packaging success (%), learning with 96 robots
number.quote: On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%.

chart.title: Phone packaging success, % of tries
chart.what: 60 tries on each of two held-out robots. Human corrections (HG-DAgger) level off with 16 robots; fleet experience (FERT) starts from a 79.2% checkpoint, dips with few robots, then climbs as robots are added.

items.name: PAR
items.headline: A Small Looped Model Stays Right at 16× Its Training Length
items.what: Training that lets a looped language model solve problems far longer than the ones it saw.
items.how: The same block of layers runs again and again; PAR trains the k-th loop to match the state after k operations (**progress-aligned targets**) and rescales the state to its first-loop norm on every loop (**norm anchoring**). Both are needed.
items.when: For tasks that update a state step by step, like tracking objects, on inputs longer than in training.

number.says: the training length: a Qwen2.5-0.5B model trained on at most 32 moves is 95.5% right at 512
number.quote: On swap-S_5, a Qwen2.5-0.5B model trained on at most 32 moves achieves 95.5\% mean full-state accuracy at 512 moves, or 16times the training length

chart.title: Full-state accuracy %, trained on up to 32 moves
chart.table: Table 1, Wang et al.; Transformer and RLT as reported by Zhang et al.
chart.what: five boxes and a run of swaps; an answer counts only if every box is right. RLT falls to 55.7% at 16 times the length; a plain Transformer and chain of thought stay near zero.

items.name: Matrix-Game 4.0
items.headline: A Playable World at 60 FPS on One Consumer GPU
items.what: A real-time playable world: a game engine holds the rules, a video model draws the picture.
items.how: A light **game engine** keeps state and rules in code and draws low-poly frames; a **coding agent** turns the player's idea into game code; the video model paints each frame in detail, four frames at a time, in one or two denoising steps.
items.when: For games or simulations whose state must not live in a video model's memory; code and weights are open.

number.says: 480p gameplay on one RTX 5090; 112 ms from key press to screen
number.quote: Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112 ms

chart.title: Key press to screen, real-time world models
chart.what: end-to-end latency as each system reports it; shorter is better. The other three ran on data-center GPUs.

items.name: OpenVLHarness
items.headline: Tools Beat Thinking Harder
items.what: An open harness that gives a vision model tools and keeps their output for the whole query.
items.how: A **capability layer** calls segmentation, depth and search through one interface and turns their output into images and short text; a **persistent multimodal memory** keeps it all by name for a coding agent to program over.
items.when: When a bigger thinking budget stops paying off: xhigh to max cost 2.7 times the tokens for 0.7 points.

number.says: Qwen3-VL-8B's average over 22 benchmarks, against the same model without tools
number.quote: including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra

chart.title: GPT-6 Luna, average score over 22 benchmarks
chart.what: more thinking lifts the bare model from 45.8 to 48.0; with tools it scores 56.5 at medium effort, for $0.92 per 1k questions against $3.17. The axis does not start at zero.

items.name: Hy-Memory-30B-A3B
items.headline: A Small Model Writes the Memory
items.what: A small memory writer, about 3B active parameters, that decides what long-term memory keeps.
items.how: It replaces the general LLM inside frameworks such as Mem0 and MemOS: what to keep, in how much detail, and how new facts update old ones. Trained by **Memory On-Policy Distillation**, then **Attributed Memory Reinforcement Learning**.
items.when: To move a memory assistant's writing step to a cheap model; it also carried over to EverMemOS, unseen in training.

number.says: average over four memory frameworks; Claude Opus 5 gets 54.62 in the same setup

chart.title: Average score as the memory writer
chart.what: the mean of four memory harnesses, changing only the model that writes the memory; Tencent's own figures.

items.name: Bridged Self-Distillation
items.headline: A Student Learns From the Teacher's Answer Alone
items.what: On-policy distillation (BSD) that passes a teacher's reasoning to a small student without the teacher's probabilities.
items.how: The teacher only writes a solution. A copy of the student that has read it (the **self-teacher**) scores the student's own attempts token by token; a verifier says which succeeded.
items.when: When the teacher uses another tokenizer or is a closed model behind an API.

number.says: over SFT in average score, for all four students; SFT fell below the base model for three of them
number.quote: BSD outperforms SFT for all four students by 3.3 to 8.6 points in average score, while SFT falls below the base model for three of them.

chart.title: Average math score, teacher Qwen3-32B
chart.what: AIME24, AIME25 and HMMT25, four tries each. Fine-tuning on the teacher's answers (SFT) leaves three students below where they started; BSD lifts all four.

items.name: RESIN
items.headline: Keeping Rival Evidence Open
items.what: RAG for questions whose answer rests on several separate chains of evidence.
items.how: The question is split into one-hop needs (**hop-wise decomposition**), a few source-linked units are fetched for each, and a small **reasoning buffer** keeps rival evidence until the final merge instead of committing early.
items.when: When plain retrieval drowns the model in noise, or graph pruning drops the right evidence too early.

number.says: context recall on all of HolisQA (how much of the needed evidence came back); answer relevancy 76.70
number.quote: On the full HolisQA benchmark, Resin achieves 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy over all questions

chart.title: Context recall on HolisQA, by domain
chart.what: the share of the evidence an answer needs that retrieval brought back. Baselines as published in the CausalRAG2 paper; only RESIN was run by its authors.

items.name: Prism
items.headline: 2K Video With Sound, Trained 2.5× Faster
items.what: Dynamic sparse attention for training video-with-audio generation directly at 2K.
items.how: Tokens are grouped into **macro-zones** in space and time; blocks are cut finer where the picture changes fast and is tightly bound to the sound, and each query's sparsity is chosen on the fly.
items.when: For high-resolution video and audio training, where full attention's cost grows quadratically with resolution.

number.says: faster training than full attention, with better generation quality
number.quote: Experiments show that Prism achieves 2.5times training speedup compared to full attention, while surpassing it in generation quality.

chart.title: Native 2K training: minutes per step, and quality
chart.what: shorter bars train faster; AQ is aesthetic quality, higher is better. SpargeAttn2 trains faster but scores lower.

items.name: Kumo Relational
items.headline: Predictions Straight From a Relational Database
items.what: A pretrained foundation model that predicts on a relational database in one forward pass, without training.
items.how: It keeps foreign keys and timestamps instead of flattening the tables into one. Attention runs within each table, then across tables as **graph attention**; it fits a task by in-context learning from up to 10000 examples, and was pretrained on fully synthetic databases.
items.when: Instead of building a separate XGBoost pipeline for each prediction such as churn; the task is written as a PQL query.

number.says: on average over gradient-boosted trees with expert-engineered features, RelBench V1 classification
number.quote: On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average.

items.name: OmniReasoning
items.headline: Questions That Need Both Sound and Picture
items.what: A benchmark, data engine and training method for questions whose answer needs both the audio and the video.
items.how: The **OmniQA** data engine writes question and answer pairs that need audio and visual evidence together, with timestamped clue chains. **MFSD** (Modality-Factored Self-Distillation) re-scores each answer with audio clues and with visual clues separately, so each token is credited to its evidence.
items.when: When a video model ignores the soundtrack; the data engine produced 112K SFT and 19K RL examples.

number.says: on OmniVideoBench over the base model Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking; score 50.0%
number.quote: improving the base model Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking by 12.8 and 9.3 percentage points, respectively

items.name: OR-License
items.headline: Agents Take On 31 Paid Consulting Jobs
items.what: A benchmark of whether LLM agents can turn real client documents into expert-level operations research solutions.
items.how: 31 instances from paid consulting work worth $3.68 million, with real requirements and data. **ORSim** plays the client; **DAQ** scores a solution against the expert's and gives zero to one that cannot be carried out.
items.when: To see where agents fall down on long jobs: mostly in framing the problem and in code.

number.says: DAQ of the strongest configuration, Grok 4.6 in the Claude Code harness; the expert's solution is 1, and 88.39% of its deliveries were feasible
number.quote: the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1

chart.title: DAQ %, under Claude Code: six of eleven models
chart.what: each delivery scored against the expert's; one that cannot be carried out scores zero. The best five models and the last one.

items.name: Mistral Large 4
items.headline: 1 Trillion Parameters, 52 Billion Active
items.what: Mistral's largest model: natively multimodal, with 1 trillion parameters and 52 billion of them active.
items.how: It is in preview on Mistral's API for now, with weights due at the end of the month; architecture and post-training details are not out yet. It was trained from scratch on 3800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Europe.
items.when: For anyone who wants a strong open-weight model on their own servers, especially for security and coding.

number.says: of DeepSWE v1.1 software tasks solved; 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4, by Mistral's own count
number.quote: scoring 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4

items.name: FocusGUI
items.headline: Where a GUI Agent Should Look
items.what: A light adapter that tells a GUI agent what to focus on at each step.
items.how: It splits the observation into channels, scores each against the step's decision and hands a frozen decoder the best evidence.
items.when: When errors pile up over many agent steps.

number.says: Type Match, 31.0% to 64.2%, averaged over four backbones
number.quote: Across four omni-modal backbones, it raises overall Type Match by +33.2 and Exact Match by 3.0\times over the frozen backbone on average

items.name: MemT-1.0
items.headline: Memory Inside the Model
items.what: Models that make memory part of their own computation, not an outside context.
items.how: A native memory block in chosen Transformer blocks is updated token by token.
items.when: For assistants and coding agents with long histories.

number.says: less persistent storage than a full KV cache at 128K tokens
number.quote: At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately 1.86\times end-to-end inference speedup and a 66\times reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache.

items.name: Headroom
items.headline: A Leaner Read for Coding Agents
items.what: Compresses what a coding agent reads, on your own machine.
items.how: A router picks a compressor for JSON, code or plain text; the originals stay local.
items.when: When a coding agent's token bill gets big.

number.says: tokens on a log dump, the FATAL line kept
number.quote: Headroom compressing a 10,144 token log dump to 1,260 tokens while preserving the FATAL line

items.name: VocabX
items.headline: A Tokenizer Built for Cost
items.what: Rebuilds a small model's tokenizer around what each token costs.
items.how: Output tokens cost more than input tokens, and the choice follows that.
items.when: For a fine-tuned small model on a single task in production.

number.says: lower measured inference cost, same base model
number.quote: cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model

also.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
also.text: A report that tests GPT-6-Astra on 12 robot benchmarks and 8 real robot setups: capable, but not yet at practical intelligence (452 HF upvotes).

also.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
also.text: The first first-person world model for both humans and robots, trained on 10k hours of human and 3k hours of robot data.

also.title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
also.text: Picks reasoning training data to fit a small target set, by matching gradients once their shared dominant directions are removed.

also.title: Graphify-Labs/graphify
also.text: A coding-agent skill that turns a codebase, its docs and SQL schemas into a queryable knowledge graph (1434 stars today).

also.text: Follows five LLM agents for 30 days in a live market: returns and measured ability often diverge.
